title: An (Extremely) Fond Farewell to Dolly Parton, Library Friend and Children’s Literacy Champion
content:
Dolly Parton, the beloved country music legend and pop culture icon who died Tuesday, was also a tireless advocate for children’s literacy whose Imagination Library was given one of Library’s highest honors, part of her long association with the national library.

In the 2021 Library of Congress Literacy Awards, the Imagination Library, an initiative of Parton’s Dollywood Foundation, was awarded the David M. Rubenstein Prize of $150,000 for the program’s phenomenal national and international success.

“Dolly Parton’s work was precisely what we envisioned this prize rewarding,” Rubenstein said. “A well-run, highly dedicated literacy program that operated both with passion and a clear sense of mission. It was a privilege to know her and her work.”

The program started in Parton’s home county in rural east Tennessee in 1995 with 1,760 children under age 5 enrolled. Each child received one free book mailed to their home monthly for up to 60 months; therefore each child would have their own library when they started first grade.

title: Making Library Events Pop: Shari Werb
content:
–This story also appears in the July/August issue of the Library of Congress Magazine.

Describe your work at the Library.

As director of the Center for Learning, Literacy and Engagement, I have the privilege of leading a team of talented colleagues who create programs and experiences that help people connect with the Library — whether they’re visiting in person, joining online or engaging from their own communities. Our work spans the offices of Library Events, Signature Programs, Informal Learning, Literary Initiatives, Visitor Engagement, and Professional Learning and Outreach Initiatives, all shaped by a deep and ongoing understanding of our audiences.

In my role, I focus on setting direction and creating the conditions for this work to thrive. That includes building consistent, audience-focused programming frameworks — like Live! At the Library, Afternoons With the Library and Family Days — that give people welcoming, predictable ways to engage. These platforms also make it easier for colleagues across the Library to bring their ideas to life and reach the audiences they care about.

title: The Supreme Court’s 1954 Brown v. Board Ruling: “A Day That Will Live in Glory”
content:
-This article also appears in the May/June issue of the Library of Congress Magazine, which focused on momentous events in the nation’s first 250 years.

The Supreme Court’s ruling in Brown v. Board of Education on May 17, 1954, was one of the most consequential decisions in American history and is exhaustively documented at the Library. A unanimous court emphatically ruled that the “separate but equal” doctrine of the 1896 Plessy v. Ferguson Supreme Court ruling — the basis for legalized segregation in the United States — was a false premise and always had been.

“We conclude that in the field of public education ‘separate but equal’ has no place,” Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote in his opinion, underlining the last phrase in his reading copy. Then he delivered the hammer blow, underlining the entire next sentence: “Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.”

The case, though focused on public schools, would apply to every facet of American life. No more “Colored Only” water fountains. The nation was entering a new era.

title: Ann Patchett Accepts Prize for American Fiction, Delights SRO National Book Festival Audience
content:
Ann Patchett accepted the Library’s 2026 Prize for American Fiction at the  National Book Festival, on stage with friend and fellow author Tayari Jones and in front of a standing-room-only crowd of more than 1,100 adoring fans, but she wasn’t entirely sure she wanted to be there.

“I feel like I’m too young for lifetime achievement,” she said, drawing a huge laugh from the crowd.

Patchett (62, for the record) overcame her tongue-in-cheek concerns that the honor was “the nail in the coffin” and accepted the award from Robert R. Newlen, the acting Librarian of Congress.

She might have been mollified by his description of one of the Library’s highest honors, given annually since 2008.

“The prize honors an American literary writer whose body of work is distinguished not only for its mastery of the art, but also for the originality and thought and imagination,” Newlen said.

Previous recipients include E.L. Doctorow, Toni Morrison, Philip Roth, Louise Erdrich, George Saunders and last year’s honoree (and Patchett’s close friend), Geraldine Brooks.

title: Inventing Telephones at the 1876 Centennial
content:
-This is a guest post by Josh Levy, a historian in the Manuscript Division. It also appears in the May/June issue of the Library of Congress Magazine.

In June of 1876, two weeks before the nation’s centennial, a young Alexander Graham Bell arrived in Philadelphia. He was staggered by what he saw. He had come to demonstrate his inventions at the Centennial Exposition, the first world’s fair hosted on American soil, with exhibits stretched massively across more than 200 buildings in Fairmount Park. “It grows upon one,” Bell wrote his soon-to-be wife, Mabel. “It is so prodigious and so wonderful … just think of having the products of all nations condensed into a few acres of buildings.”

Like any of the era’s world’s fairs, the exhibition was a breathless celebration of progress, a spectacle of industry and commerce, art and culture. Nearly 10 million visitors attended. Those visitors may easily have passed by Bell’s telephone, but the impression of the nation’s burgeoning industrial power was unmistakable.

title: The Source: Where Curiosity Sparks Discovery
content:
The drawers from the card catalog are meant to surprise you.

Open one, and a tornado from “The Wizard of Oz” swirls to life. Another reveals a rocket launch. A third shows Rosa Parks’ pancake recipe.

At The Source, the Library’s first-of-its-kind experiential research gallery for young people, the familiar wooden card catalog becomes an entry point into history, inviting visitors to explore the past not as something dusted off in a dog-eared textbook but as something they can actively discover.

Here, the past unfolds in multiple formats. Voices echo from across time, and collection items pull young visitors into the role of budding researchers. From the moment they enter the ground floor of the Jefferson Building, they can ask questions, make connections and explore history through a blend of nostalgia and modern technology.

title: Was “Charlotte Temple” America’s First Bestselling Novel?
content:
—This is a guest post by Rebecca Rose, a reference specialist in Duplication Services. It also appears in the July/August issue of the Library of Congress Magazine.

Before bestseller lists and BookTok, there was “Charlotte Temple,” an 18th-century novel that created one of America’s first and most lasting literary fandoms. Generations of readers devoured the tragic story of Charlotte, a young English girl seduced and abandoned by a British soldier during the American Revolution.

The Library’s Rare Book and Special Collections Division holds at least a dozen copies of “Charlotte Temple,” including an 1802 edition in which a later reader inserted newspaper clippings describing how, by the end of the 19th century, the New York City grave of a real-life woman named Charlotte Temple became a pilgrimage site for readers who mistook her for the fictional Charlotte.

title: American Women Fight for Their Own Independence
content:
—This is as guest post by Elizabeth A. Novara, a historian in the Manuscript Division. It also appears in the May/June issue of the Library of Congress Magazine, which is devoted to the celebration of the nation’s 250th birthday.

The Declaration of Independence inspired many American women to demand their rights.

The most famous instance is likely the nation’s first women’s rights convention in Seneca Falls, New York, in July 1848. At this meeting of over 300 persons, suffragist Elizabeth Cady Stanton read her now-famous “Declaration of Sentiments” protesting women’s inferior legal status and listing 11 resolutions for the moral, economic and political equality of women, the most radical of which demanded “the elective franchise.”

Fast forward to 1876, when the nation celebrated the 100th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence with the Centennial Exposition, a massive world’s fair held in Philadelphia that drew nearly 10 million visitors for an exuberant six-month celebration of American progress and patriotism.

title: Ray White Retires … After a Quick 44.5 Years
content:
Let’s check in with 1982.

“E.T.” landed in theaters and called home. Something called “emoticons” were posted by a computer scientist and so began the creation story of emojis. CDs appeared in record stores. And the Library’s Music Division hired Raymond White, a fresh-faced young man from University of Maryland with degrees in history and vocal performance, to a permanent position.

And lo, for all the days in the world since then until the one at the very end of this month, Ray White has been a fixture at the Library of Congress. He retires at the close of business on Friday, July 31, a mere 44.5 years after he officially started. We are sorry he is leaving so soon but will wish him the best anyhow.

Ray has delighted patrons, scholars and guests of the Library with his knowledge of the field, encompassing everything from Beethoven to Broadway show tunes, including delightful asides and bon mots about great pieces of art or how simple little songs became big hits. Though he does much work behind the scenes, he is best known for his storytelling in presenting items for guests, be they students or VIPs, to marvel over.
creator: Neely Tucker
sourceDescription: Stories from the Library of Congress

title: Two Thousand Years of “The Odyssey” at the Library
content:
Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster adaptation of “The Odyssey” introduces the epic poem attributed to Homer to a new generation of moviegoers, turning a nearly 3,000-year-old story into a fresh cultural touchstone.

The Library’s vast collections, covering centuries of time, document how artists, cartographers and translators around the world have translated and reimagined Odysseus’ journey anew. From medieval engravings to graphic novels, the Library’s holdings document how each generation seems to find fresh meaning in the mythical, decade-long struggle of the Greek hero to return home to his wife, Penelope, and son, Telemachus, following the Trojan War.

The 12,000-line prose poem originated in an oral tradition more than 2,800 years ago in ancient Greece and was performed at festivals for hundreds of years. It uses monsters, murder, war, gods and disasters to pose timeless questions about loyalty and perseverance, resilience, temptation, loss and, above all, the universal search for belonging.

The Library’s holdings on work attributed to Homer go back about 2,000 years, with a papyrus fragment from “The Iliad,” the precursor to “The Odyssey,” and then continue as the centuries go by.
